title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Elimination—Toileting, Urinary & Bowel Care
html:
Urinary and bowel elimination are private, essential functions that affect comfort, mobility, skin integrity, hydration, sleep, and dignity. The RN provides timely, respectful assistance while assessing patterns and changes. Care begins with the client's usual routine, current condition, ability to reach the toilet safely, and preferences—not with assumptions about what is normal.

Learning goals

  • Collect objective and subjective urinary and bowel-elimination data.
  • Support safe, dignified toileting and continence care.
  • Recognize cues of urinary retention, infection, constipation, diarrhea, and bleeding.
  • Maintain an indwelling urinary catheter safely within orders and policy.
  • Evaluate whether an elimination plan is effective and tolerated.

Assess the pattern and the change

Ask about the client's usual frequency, urgency, dysuria, difficulty starting a stream, incontinence, urine appearance, and recent changes. For bowel assessment, ask about the usual routine, date and characteristics of the last bowel movement, abdominal symptoms, bowel control, diet and fluid pattern, activity, and medications that can affect elimination. Document measurable observations such as intake and output when ordered, stool appearance, episodes of incontinence, and the client's symptoms. Use the client's language with dignity and clarify unfamiliar words.

Trend, not assumption
New suprapubic discomfort, inability to void, a distended lower abdomen, painful urination, fever, sudden diarrhea, black tarry stool, bright-red blood, or a major change from baseline needs focused assessment and the appropriate escalation—not a label assigned from one cue alone.

Promote safe, dignified toileting

Offer regular opportunities for toileting and respond to call lights promptly. Protect privacy, provide adequate time, preserve modesty, and use the safest transfer plan or assistive equipment. Support the position and environment that best fit the client and care plan. Cleanse and dry the perineal area after incontinence, protect skin as ordered, and avoid shaming language. Encourage fluids, fiber, activity, or a bowel routine only when these measures are appropriate to the client's plan, condition, and prescribed restrictions.

Recognize retention, constipation, diarrhea, and urgent cues

Urinary retention can present with inability to void, frequent small voids, suprapubic fullness or discomfort, restlessness, or a distended bladder. Constipation can involve a change from the person's usual pattern, hard stool, straining, abdominal discomfort, or reduced stool passage. Diarrhea can create fluid loss, skin injury, infection-control, and urgency concerns. The RN assesses the whole pattern, reviews relevant medication and procedure history, follows orders for tests such as a bladder scan or specimen collection, and communicates concerning findings.

Severe abdominal pain or distention, repeated vomiting, syncope, hypotension, a rigid abdomen, significant rectal bleeding, or black tarry stool can indicate urgent deterioration. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and mental status, then activate the required urgent response. Do not give an unprescribed laxative, antidiarrheal, or enema to make a concerning problem disappear.

Indwelling urinary catheter: protect the closed system

An indwelling catheter is used only for an appropriate indication and for no longer than needed. Verify the order and assess ongoing need according to policy. Maintain a closed drainage system, keep tubing free of kinks and dependent loops, secure the catheter as directed, and keep the collection bag below bladder level and off the floor. Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate precautions when manipulating the system. Empty the bag using the approved technique and a clean designated container; avoid contaminating the outlet.

Never disconnect the system, irrigate the catheter, collect a specimen, or replace equipment except as ordered and within policy. New leakage, disconnection, obstruction, no expected drainage, fever, pain, or visible blood calls for assessment and the prescribed escalation. A catheter is not a substitute for routine incontinence care or convenient toileting.

Evaluate the plan

Reassess comfort, ability to toilet safely, urinary output when ordered, voiding or stool pattern, symptoms, skin condition, hydration clues, and the client's goals. Document response to interventions and communicate trends that are worsening or not meeting the expected outcome. Elimination care is successful when it supports physiologic needs, safety, and dignity together.

Clinical example

After surgery, a client reports painful lower-abdominal fullness and has made several small voids but cannot empty the bladder. The RN assesses the pattern and suprapubic area, reviews the postoperative plan, verifies the relevant order, obtains a bladder scan if authorized, and communicates the findings. Repeatedly telling the client to “try harder” would delay assessment of a possible retention problem.
